profile.reading:
Per Vantage Data Centers' own facility page, this building, WA11, sits on Vantage's Quincy, WA campus at 2101 M Street NE, Quincy, WA 98848. Vantage describes the 68-acre campus as three data centers totaling 775,000 square feet and 89 megawatts of critical IT load, powered via Grant County PUD with N+1 mechanical redundancy and EPA Tier II generators the operator says achieve a 90% emissions reduction. WA11 specifically is cited on the page as holding Uptime Institute Tier III certification for both Design Documents and Constructed Facility, Tier III Gold for Operational Sustainability, and LEED Gold from the US Green Building Council, the only one of the three Quincy buildings with certifications individually named. No individual sqft or MW breakdown per building is published.

Vantage is a private, Denver, Colorado-headquartered operator; DigitalBridge acquired the company in March 2017, and in January 2024 Vantage announced a $6.4 billion equity investment round led by DigitalBridge and Silver Lake. Quincy, in Grant County, Washington, is one of the country's oldest hydro-powered data center hubs, drawing operators for decades with the Columbia Basin's cheap, abundant hydroelectric power from Grant County PUD's Columbia and Priest Rapids dams, alongside Microsoft, Yahoo, Sabey, and NTT DATA facilities also tracked elsewhere in this registry.

Quincy's data center cluster, including Vantage's WA11/WA12/WA13 campus, has drawn periodic scrutiny over Grant County PUD's discounted industrial power rates for large users relative to residential ratepayers, a recurring subject at PUD commission meetings and in Washington state legislative discussion of data center electricity consumption and grid capacity planning. Grant County's data center campuses sit within land the city and county have zoned for industrial and manufacturing use, and local officials have continued to permit sector expansion given its role as a major employer and property-tax contributor for a city of roughly 8,000 residents. Washington state has periodically debated adjusting or sunsetting a sales-and-use-tax exemption program for data centers that has been credited with drawing much of this Central Washington cluster, including Microsoft, Yahoo, Sabey, Intuit, and Vantage facilities, to Quincy over the past two decades.

reading.body:
Vantage WA11 is one building in a three-building campus in Quincy, Washington totaling 89 MW of critical IT load and 775,000 square feet, though the operator does not publish how that capacity divides among the three buildings. At typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, the 89 MW campus-wide figure would correspond to roughly 2,200 racks, but WA11's individual share is not stated. The campus ranks third among Washington state's 46 mapped data center facilities by published capacity and represents nearly the entire 60 MW of publicly disclosed capacity in the state.

WA11 holds Tier III certification, qualifying it for three concurrent maintenance windows without downtime to critical systems. The building also carries LEED Gold status, indicating it meets energy efficiency standards but not specifying renewable energy sourcing. Neither certification reveals what workloads the operator markets to tenants or whether the campus is currently fully leased.

The lack of building-level capacity breakdown leaves WA11's actual scale within the campus opaque. Washington's grid position and hydropower access have made it a significant draw for data center operators in recent years, but the state publishes minimal detailed capacity data, making this campus one of very few facilities there with any disclosed figure at all.
